Convergence, split-brain and push ordering as a distributed-systems problem were adjudicated by fd-distsys-harvest-splitbrain and fd-distributed-sync-data-integrity in earlier passes. Yours is the accounting question they do not ask: which book is the authority for a figure, and what the figure becomes when that book is rewritten.
The rename cascade, marketplace rows, npm versions and settings keys belong to fd-release-engineering-cascade; touch them only where a rename moves a book of original entry or a retention list.
decision_lens: Take each field the plan writes into an index record and answer three questions in writing: which book supplies it (a harvest sighting row, a ledger attribution row, the prior index.jsonl, agent frontmatter), what the merge does when that source is absent on this run, and whether the absence is distinguishable in the output from a genuine nil. A field recomputed from CURRENT sightings is not accretive however loudly the record says accessioned_at; say so, and name the run that empties it. Then set the two branch journals side by side at the instant each of Tasks 14, 15, 23 and 24 executes and enumerate the items in transit. Finally, refuse every destruction whose authority is checked at a different moment than the destruction itself: name the entry, the agreement (which SHA, pushed to which ref, verified when) and the signed list, and say which of the three the plan checks at a moment other than --apply. Severity follows the paper: a voucher burned against an entry that cannot be reconstructed is P0.
distance_rationale: The counting-house has no lineage to software and none of its words — no merge, no replica, no idempotence, no conflict resolution. What it has is five centuries of hard experience with the exact situation this plan builds: two sets of books kept by two clerks in two places, one ledger that both must agree with, and a decision about when a piece of paper may be burned. The discipline named its failure modes long before there was a way to automate them, and the names have no software equivalent that would occur to an engineer reviewing this plan: the item in transit (written in one house, not yet posted in the other, and not an error), the cut-off error (a real event posted to the wrong period because the clock that decided was not the clock that mattered), the double posting, the misposting by account NAME where two accounts share a name, the compensating error that leaves a trial balance in perfect agreement while both sides are wrong, the nil balance that is not a closed account, and window dressing — a figure made true only at the instant it is looked at. Each of those is a live hazard in Tasks 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 23 and 24, and none of them is visible from a distributed-systems framing, which asks about conflict and convergence and therefore stops as soon as the plan says 'accretive'. The counting-house asks a different and sharper question: not 'do the two copies converge' but 'which book is the authority for this figure, and what happens to the figure when that book is rewritten'.
expected_isomorphisms: Books of original entry = data/harvest/clavain.jsonl and data/harvest/zklw.jsonl, each written wholesale by its own machine's scan. The ledger = data/generated/index.jsonl. Posting rules = the merge semantics in Task 9 (which fields carry forward, which are recomputed from current sightings). The voucher = the .claude/agents/fd-*.md file itself, which Task 23 burns. Retention authority = data/prune-targets.txt reviewed and committed by a human. The certificate of destruction = data/reports/<date>-prune-<machine>.md. Books closed and agreed with the other house = Task 23 precondition (2), HEAD == origin/main, and the registry SHA written into every prune commit. Items in transit = everything one machine has harvested, committed or deleted that the other has not yet pulled at the instant Tasks 14, 15, 23 and 24 run. Cut-off = precondition (4), newest fd-*.md mtime against the harvest file's timestamp. Control account against subsidiary ledger = python3 -m harvest audit (index vs body files vs embedding rows vs edge endpoints). Trial balance agreeing through compensating errors = a record and its body file lost together, which produces no orphan and therefore no audit failure. Posting by name = Task 10 attributing ledger rows on lens == name, while Task 12 clusters several distinct records that share a name and Task 3 resolves a name to a head. Nil balance versus closed account = on_disk: false with sightings: 0 against a record that was never accessioned. Turnover versus balance = sightings_seen against sightings. Memorandum entries that must not inflate turnover = the reuse-sighting rows of Task 8.
focus: Whether the two houses' books can be made to agree, and whether the paper Task 23 burns is covered by an entry that is posted, agreed and listed. Every field of an index.jsonl record traced back to the book of original entry that supplies it and forward to the run that overwrites it — with particular attention to which fields survive the disappearance of the sighting that carried them, and to what the audit would still call clean.
name: fd-bookkeeping-reconciliation
persona: Apply the perspective of a house bookkeeper closing the year for a merchant with two counting-houses and one ledger. A figure is not trusted because it is written neatly; it is traced to the book of original entry, and that book to the voucher behind it. Two clerks in two cities always disagree at any instant, and the disagreement is not an error but a list of items in transit that must be enumerated rather than waved away. Nothing is corrected by erasure — a wrong entry is answered by a dated contra entry, so the mistake survives alongside its correction. No voucher is burned until three things hold at once: the entry is posted, the ledger is agreed with the other house at a stated date and reference, and the item stands on a list a principal has signed. A trial balance that agrees is the least reassuring thing in the room; compensating errors agree perfectly.
review_areas: Which fields are actually accretive. Task 9 makes accessioned_at, sightings_seen and on_disk survive a vanished sighting, but machines, repos, cohort, lineage, domains, spec_path, summary, tier, use_count, last_used and drive_uses are all specified as computed from current sightings ('max across non-reuse sightings', 'first sighting with a spec wins', 'sorted union'). Walk one record through Task 23's deletion of its only file and then through the next harvest-and-push.sh run on that machine, and state field by field what the record still says. The prune report cites the registry as the reason deletion was safe; say what the registry still holds about the deleted file.

Books of original entry that are rewritten. data/harvest/<machine>.jsonl is regenerated wholesale by that machine's scan, and Task 10 recomputes stats and rewrites data/generated/attributions.jsonl from whatever attribution rows the current harvest files contain. Ask what happens to attributions, lineage and cohort whose only witness was a melange run directory or heat-ledger that has since been deleted, moved, or lives in a repo the other machine does not have — and whether hit_rate, smoothed_hit_rate and therefore cluster head selection can silently regress between runs.

Items in transit and cut-off. Read scripts/harvest-and-push.sh in Task 22 as the reconciliation procedure it is: pull --ff-only, six subcommands, commit, then push with a pull --rebase --autostash retry whose failure is swallowed by || true. Both machines rewrite the same sorted index.jsonl. State what a rebase of one machine's data commit onto the other's does to the merged record set, what the trap's git checkout -- data && git clean -fdq data destroys when the failure happens at a step other than the one intended, and whether Task 23 precondition (4)'s mtime comparison survives a git checkout, a clone, a worktree, or the two machines' clocks.

Posting by name where accounts share one. Task 10 attributes on lens == name; Task 12 clusters distinct records (distinct bodies, distinct hashes, distinct ids) that share a name or exceed a cosine, then picks the head by the smoothed hit-rate those name-level postings produced; Task 3 resolves a name to a head; Task 16 materializes by name. Trace one name used by two different bodies in different repos through stats -> edges -> head selection -> resolve, and say whose findings paid for whose rank, and whether the same finding is counted once or once per record. Do the same for a fusion lens whose parents' names appear in the ledger.

What the trial balance cannot catch. Task 12's audit checks body file and embedding row per record, orphans in the other direction, edge endpoints, one head per cluster and the hash recipe. Enumerate the losses that leave it clean: a record and its body file removed together, a duplicate body_hash written as two records, sightings_seen going down, reuse_sightings counted into sightings after all, attributions attached to a name no record carries, a machine silently missing from every record because its harvest file was empty rather than absent. Name the control totals the audit does not carry and where they would have to be written.

Destruction under authority, against the real tree. Run the candidate rule of Task 23 against ~/projects as it actually is: piles whose directory is not a git repository root (~/projects/Sylveste/land-jawncite-spec carries hundreds of files and sits inside the Sylveste repo, whose main is protected and whose shared checkout is on another session's branch), the -sessions / -f2 / -spike-* suffix rule and which path segment it is applied to, untracked piles where rm leaves no commit and the only record is a report committed in a different repository, repos sitting on a feature branch where the prune commit lands and can be deleted with the branch, and the human-review gate — say who verifies that prune-targets.txt at --apply time is the file the human signed.

severity_examples.condition: File the finding when the plan's merge semantics do not name a preservation rule for a field on a record with zero current sightings, and quote the sentence that recomputes it. Do not file it for sightings, on_disk or accessioned_at, which Task 9 handles explicitly.
severity_examples.scenario: Task 23 deletes the last fd-*.md file of record gen:fd-x@1a2b3c4d, citing the registry as the reason deletion is safe. The next scheduled harvest-and-push.sh run on that machine rewrites data/harvest/clavain.jsonl with no row for that file, and merge recomputes the record from current sightings: machines and repos become empty or lose that machine, tier / use_count / last_used are described as 'max across non-reuse sightings' with no rule for zero sightings, cohort is 'from the first sighting with a spec' and there is none, domains is a union of nothing. Only accessioned_at, sightings_seen, on_disk and the body file are stated to survive. The audit passes: the body file and the embedding row are both still there, so nothing is orphaned. The prune report that justified the deletion cites repos and machines fields that are now empty.

severity_examples.condition: File it against the script as written in Task 22, quoting the trap line and the loop that sets STEP. Say which of Tasks 15, 22, 23 and 24 invoke it and what state each of them holds under data/ at that moment.
severity_examples.scenario: The trap in scripts/harvest-and-push.sh fires on any non-zero exit and runs git checkout -q -- data && git clean -fdq data. STEP is set to pull before the first command, so a failure of git pull --ff-only — the commonest failure, since both machines commit to the same sorted index.jsonl and main moves under them — reaches the trap and discards every uncommitted and untracked file under data/ that was there before the script started, including a Mac-side harvest a human was mid-way through reviewing before a prune. The failure log records rc and STEP, not what was discarded, and the next line of defence, Task 23 precondition (1), reads a now-clean tree and reports everything in order.

severity_examples.condition: File it only after confirming from the plan that stats attributes on name and that the cluster rule accepts identical name without a cosine test. Say whether the double-count also reaches registry_stats and the reuse log, and give the smallest change of posting rule that fixes it.
severity_examples.scenario: Two different lenses named fd-authplatform-migration exist in two repos with different bodies and therefore different ids. The melange heat ledgers record findings against the NAME. Task 10 gives both records the same findings, upheld, adjudicated and smoothed_hit_rate. Task 12 puts them in one cluster (identical name is sufficient) and selects the head by smoothed_hit_rate, which is now a tie broken by id — the lens that earned the adjudications may lose to the copy that earned nothing, and either way registry_stats reports the findings twice across the two records. Task 3's name resolution then serves whichever record won, and Task 16 materializes it for every future reuse.

source_domain: Double-entry bookkeeping and the closing of the books — the mercantile clerical craft codified in the Genoese commune accounts and the Datini house books a century before Pacioli printed it in 1494, and refined since by five centuries of branch-house practice and statutory audit. Its apparatus: the book of original entry (waste book, journal) kept where the event happens and never rewritten; posting from that book to the ledger under a rule; the control account that must agree with the subsidiary ledger behind it; the trial balance; the branch-and-home-office reconciliation whose whole method is the enumeration of items in transit; the cut-off that decides which period an entry falls in; correction only by a dated contra entry, never an erasure; the voucher retained as the authority for the entry; and the destruction of vouchers only under a written retention authority, after the books are closed and agreed, item by item on a list a principal has signed.
success_hints: Trace, do not characterize. Every finding names the field, the book that supplies it, the sentence of the plan that posts it, and the run that overwrites it. A finding that says the merge 'may lose data' without naming a field and a run is not a finding.

Read the real tree before asserting anything about the sweep: find the fd-*.md piles under ~/projects, check which of their directories are git repository roots (git -C <dir> rev-parse --show-toplevel), which are on a branch other than main, and whether the pile is tracked. Quote counts you measured, not the plan's round numbers.

Separate a nil from an absence in your own writing as strictly as you demand the plan does. If a check could not be run — zklw unreachable, a repo missing, ssh gated — say could not look, and never let that read as nothing there.

The findings already folded (the 'Review findings' tables, melange f-NNN and melange-2 f-NNN) are out of bounds unless the fold itself is wrong or incomplete. f-028's accretive index is the fold most worth re-testing: it fixed record survival, and the question is whether it fixed FIELD survival.

Where a destruction depends on an agreement, state the three moments separately — when the agreement is checked, when the list is signed, when the file is removed — and say what can change in between. Most prune findings are really findings about the gap between those moments.

Prefer one traced record over five plausible ones. Pick a real record shape from the plan's Task 9 JSON block and carry it through scan, merge, stats, edges, audit, prune and the next harvest, writing what each step leaves.
